questions.explanation: Colonists accepted Parliament's authority to regulate trade but rejected direct taxes voted by a body in which they held no seats, so the slogan tied taxation to representation.
questions.hint: What links paying a tax to having a vote?
questions.learningObjective: explain the no-taxation-without-representation claim

options.text: Colonists owed taxes because the king protected them

options.misconception: reverses the colonists' position on trade laws
options.text: Colonists rejected all trade regulation by Parliament
Colonists should pay no tax voted by a body where they hold no seats

options.misconception: invents a colonial demand for a new king
options.text: Colonists demanded a separate American king to approve taxes

provenance.author: bank-team-hss-c

questions.stem: Read the passage, then answer: a Boston merchant writes that his goods pay duties set in London, where no colonist sits or votes. Which principle does his complaint express?

stimulus.body: In 1768 a Boston merchant wrote that every chest in his warehouse paid a duty fixed across the ocean. No colonist had sat in the chamber that voted the duty, and no colonial assembly had approved it. He asked why men who held no seat should open their purses at another body's command.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY

questions.explanation: The pamphlet restates the social contract: rulers hold power only by the consent of the governed, and the people may withdraw it when rulers break the bargain.
questions.hint: Who gives rulers their power in this argument?
questions.learningObjective: identify the social-contract idea behind revolution

options.text: Kings rule by divine command that no subject may question
Government rests on the people's consent and may be changed by them
The strongest army earns a permanent right to rule

options.misconception: treats the contract as a trade treaty
options.text: Colonies must buy their freedom with a fixed payment

provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used
provenance.author: bank-team-hss-c

questions.stem: A 1774 pamphlet argues that a people lend power to their rulers the way a master lends tools to a servant, and may take them back when the servant turns tyrant. Which Enlightenment idea does the pamphlet use?

stimulus.body: A pamphlet printed in Philadelphia in 1774 declared that no ruler owns his subjects. Power, it said, is lent by the people the way a master lends tools to a servant, and a people may reclaim what they lent when the servant turns the tools against them.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY

questions.explanation: The First and Second Estates held privileges and exemptions while the Third Estate, which included nearly everyone, carried the direct taxes, so the fiscal burden fell hardest on those with the least power.
questions.hint: Who paid the direct taxes?
questions.learningObjective: explain estate inequality as a cause of the French Revolution

options.text: The Third Estate paid direct taxes while the privileged estates escaped them
Clergy and nobles paid all taxes while commoners paid none
Each estate paid an equal fixed share of royal taxes
Foreign bankers taxed all three estates equally

provenance.author: bank-team-hss-c

questions.stem: A village notebook from 1788 lists a farmer's payments to the crown while the nearby abbey and manor pay nothing on their great lands. What unfair arrangement does the notebook reveal?

stimulus.body: A village notebook from 1788 records one farmer's payments to the royal treasury, item by item. On the facing page the writer notes that the great abbey and the manor beside it, with their wide fields, paid nothing on the same levy because prayer and sword excused their orders from the tax.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY

questions.explanation: The declaration proclaimed liberty, property, security, and resistance to oppression as natural rights no government could lawfully strip away.

questions.learningObjective: state the natural-rights claims of the 1789 declaration

options.text: It fixed a single fair rate of tax for all provinces
It granted noble titles to veteran soldiers

options.misconception: confuses the declaration with a church decree

It named liberty, property, security, and resistance to oppression as natural rights

questions.stem: In the assembly hall a deputy reads aloud a new charter: men are born free and equal in rights, and law must guard their liberty and goods. Which document is being read?

stimulus.body: In August 1789 deputies in Paris adopted a short charter. It announced that all men are born free and remain equal in rights, and that every political association exists to preserve liberty, property, security, and resistance to oppression.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Declaration of the Rights of Man

questions.learningObjective: explain the symbolic meaning of the Bastille's fall

options.text: It proved that foreign armies had conquered Paris
It showed royal power could fall to organized popular force

options.misconception: treats a weapons raid as a peace treaty
options.text: It marked the king's signed peace with the assembly

options.misconception: confuses the fortress with a grain store
options.text: It ended the bread shortage in a single day

questions.stem: On a July morning in 1789 thousands of Parisians stormed an old royal fortress that stored arms and gunpowder. Why did this attack become the great symbol of the revolution?

stimulus.body: On 14 July 1789 a great crowd gathered before an aged royal fortress in Paris where gunpowder was stored. Its walls had once locked away the king's prisoners. By nightfall the crowd had broken in, seized the powder, and pulled the hated stones down.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY

questions.explanation: Revolutionary tribunals sent thousands to the guillotine on suspicion of disloyalty, showing the movement defending itself with organized state terror.

questions.learningObjective: analyze the Reign of Terror as revolutionary state violence

options.misconception: confuses the Terror with foreign war
options.text: It proves invading armies controlled Paris in 1793
It shows courts freed all prisoners out of pity
It shows revolutionaries executing suspected enemies to save the republic
It proves slavery ended because masters feared Paris mobs

questions.stem: Court records from 1794 show Paris tribunals condemning shopkeepers, priests, and deputies after brief hearings, all in the name of saving the republic. What does this pattern reveal about the Terror?

stimulus.body: Between 1793 and 1794 special tribunals in Paris tried thousands of suspects in hurried sessions. Shopkeepers, priests, and even deputies mounted the scaffold after brief hearings, while officials announced that fear would guard the republic against its hidden enemies.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY

questions.explanation: The code ended feudal dues, made all men equal before the law, protected property, and rewarded merit, carrying revolutionary legal principles into every conquered land.
questions.hint: What happened to feudal privilege under the code?
questions.learningObjective: explain how the Napoleonic Code spread revolutionary law

options.text: It imposed legal equality, property rights, and careers open to merit
It restored feudal dues and closed offices to commoners

questions.stem: A prefect in a conquered province reports that new courts now judge noble and peasant by the same book, and that old manor dues can no longer be collected. Which reform is the prefect describing?

stimulus.body: After 1804 French officials carried a single bound law book into each conquered province. Its pages abolished the old manor dues, declared every man equal before the courts, protected property, and opened public offices to talent instead of birth.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY

questions.explanation: French occupation insulted local pride and proved that a people could resist an emperor, so Spaniards, Germans, and Russians developed their own patriotic movements in reply.
questions.hint: How did occupied peoples react to foreign rule?
questions.learningObjective: analyze Napoleonic occupation as a spur to rival nationalisms

options.text: Occupied peoples abandoned their languages and customs forever
Spaniards and Germans welcomed permanent French rule
Local fighters joined France to crush their own kings
Occupation awakened patriotic resistance movements against the French

provenance.author: bank-team-hss-c

questions.stem: Spanish villagers ambushed French columns while German writers praised their own language and past, all during the years of Napoleon's empire. What unintended result of French conquest do these reactions show?

stimulus.body: From Madrid to Berlin the French emperor placed his brothers on thrones and taxed the land for his wars. Spanish villagers ambushed his columns in the hills, and German writers who once admired Paris began to praise their own tongue and history instead.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY

questions.explanation: Beginning in 1791 enslaved workers rose across Saint-Domingue, defeated the planters and then French armies, and founded Haiti in 1804, the only state born of a successful slave revolt.
questions.hint: Who rose, and what state did they found?
questions.learningObjective: identify the Haitian Revolution as a successful slave revolt

options.misconception: confuses Haiti with a French colony kept
options.text: Planters crushed the rising and kept the colony enslaved
Enslaved workers overthrew the planters and founded independent Haiti

options.misconception: credits a foreign king with liberation
options.text: A European king freed the colony as a gift to its people
Planters voted to free workers without any revolt

questions.stem: Fires lit the night sky over the northern plain of Saint-Domingue in 1791 as thousands of enslaved workers left the plantations with blades and torches. How did this uprising end?

stimulus.body: In August 1791 fires crowned the hills of the northern plain of Saint-Domingue. Thousands of enslaved workers marched from the plantations with blades and torches, burning the great houses. Twelve years later their generals had beaten every army sent against them, and the free state of Haiti stood in the colony's place.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY

questions.explanation: France proclaimed liberty universal while its richest colony ran on enslaved labor, so the Haitian struggle exposed the gap between revolutionary ideals and plantation reality.
questions.hint: What did Paris promise, and what did the colony practice?
questions.learningObjective: analyze the clash between French liberty ideals and colonial slavery

options.misconception: claims the colony had no slavery
options.text: Saint-Domingue used only free wage labor before 1791
Paris never promised liberty to any of its subjects
Universal liberty proclaimed in Paris contradicted slavery that enriched the colony
Haitian planters taught Paris the meaning of liberty

provenance.author: bank-team-hss-c

questions.stem: A rebel officer in Saint-Domingue read the Paris promise that all men are free, then looked out over cane fields worked by chained gangs. What contradiction did his experience expose?

stimulus.body: A rebel officer in Saint-Domingue kept a folded Paris newspaper promising liberty to all men. The same week he watched chained gangs cut cane on a great estate whose sugar filled the king's ships. He asked his comrades how the same nation could print the promise and pocket the profits.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY

options.text: He led armies that freed much of South America from Spain

options.text: He sailed to restore the Spanish king's full power

questions.stem: A Caracas-born officer crossed the Andes with a ragged army, losing mules and men to cold, then descended to win battles on the Pacific side. Which leader and achievement are described?

stimulus.body: A Caracas-born officer led his ragged army over the freezing Andes passes, losing mules and men to the cold. Descending the far slope, his troops shattered royalist forces in battle after battle, until new republics bearing free constitutions replaced the viceroys' rule.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY

questions.explanation: American-born Creoles owned land and wealth yet were shut out of the highest offices, which the crown reserved for peninsular Spaniards, breeding deep resentment.
questions.hint: Which offices were closed to Creoles?
questions.learningObjective: explain Creole grievances under Spanish rule

options.text: Creoles held every high office by ancient right
Creoles were born in Spain and ruled the colonies gladly
Creoles owned no land and paid no taxes at all
Wealthy Creoles were barred from top offices reserved for Spanish-born men

questions.stem: A Lima landowner writes bitterly that though his family has held its estate for a century, every viceroy and high judge arrives by ship from Spain. What colonial grievance fills his letter?

stimulus.body: A wealthy Lima landowner wrote that his family had worked its estate for a hundred years, yet every viceroy, governor, and high judge arrived by ship from across the sea. Men born in America, he complained, might grow rich but would never wear the highest robes of command.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY

options.text: Brazil fought a twenty-year war against Spanish armies
Brazil kept a monarchy under its own prince with little warfare
Enslaved workers seized power and founded a republic at once
Brazil refused independence and remained fully ruled from Lisbon

questions.stem: On a riverbank in 1822 a prince raised his sword and declared Brazil free, yet he kept his crown and ruled as emperor afterward. How did Brazil's break differ from Spanish America's?

stimulus.body: On a riverbank in 1822 the Portuguese prince raised his sword and cried that Brazil was free. No great war followed. The prince kept his crown, ministers bowed to an emperor instead of a distant king, and the plantations worked on as before.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY

questions.stem: In 1815 well-dressed diplomats in Vienna redrew the map, seated fallen kings back on thrones, and promised to meet again whenever revolution stirred. What was their shared goal?

stimulus.body: Through the winter of 1815 the victors over Napoleon danced and bargained in Vienna. They redrew borders with rulers' pencils, seated fallen kings back upon their thrones, and pledged to march together whenever the spirit of revolution raised its head again.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY

options.text: Loyalty owed only to a king's family line

questions.stem: A Milan newspaper in 1848 declares that people who share a tongue, songs, and memory of past glory should no longer obey foreign emperors. Which idea fills its columns?

stimulus.body: A Milan newspaper in 1848 told its readers that they shared one tongue, one faith, and the memory of ancient glory. Why, it asked, should men who sang the same songs obey ministers in a distant foreign capital instead of governing themselves?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY

questions.learningObjective: analyze nationalism as both unifying and fragmenting

questions.stem: Compare the two scenes: Turin volunteers drilling to join their state with Lombardy, and Prague students demanding schools in their own Slav tongue free of Vienna. What double effect of nationalism do they show?

stimulus.body: In Turin volunteers drilled with the dream of joining their small state to Lombardy and beyond. In the same decade Prague students petitioned for schools in their own Slav tongue, refusing the language of Vienna. Both crowds sang of a people that should rule itself.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY

questions.explanation: Years of pamphlets, petitions, boycotts, and testimony exposed the trade's cruelty, while revolts in the colonies and shifting profits weakened its defenders, until Parliament acted in 1807 and 1833.

questions.learningObjective: explain the abolition of the British slave trade and slavery

questions.stem: London shops in 1807 displayed petitions with thousands of names beside drawings of chained figures in a ship's hold, and news of colonial revolts filled the papers. What combination finally ended the trade and then slavery itself?

stimulus.body: In 1807 London shops displayed long petitions beside drawings of chained figures packed in a ship's hold. Preachers denounced the trade, sailors testified to its cruelty, and news of burning plantations arrived from the colonies. Parliament first banned the trade, then in 1833 voted slavery itself down.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY

Slavery continued unchanged because nobody opposed it

questions.stem: Two historians debate: one says conscience ended slavery, the other says profits did. The record shows packed petitions, revolts, and also falling sugar earnings. Which judgment best fits the evidence?

stimulus.body: Two historians quarreled in print. One wrote that conscience alone broke the chains, pointing to petitions and sermons. The other answered that falling sugar earnings and the cost of guarding plantations did the work, pointing to ledgers. Both cited true facts from the same years.

questions.stem: A Paris writer answered the declaration of the rights of man with a declaration of the rights of woman, asking by what reason liberty stops at half the nation. What was her argument?

stimulus.body: A Paris writer answered the famous declaration with one of her own, addressed to women. If men hold liberty by nature, she asked, by what reason does nature halt at half the nation? She demanded that mothers and daughters share the citizenship promised to fathers and sons.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY

questions.explanation: Across the Atlantic, movements spoke the language of liberty and rights, faced bankrupt crowns or rigid hierarchies, and mobilized crowds and armies, even as their outcomes for enslaved people and women diverged.

questions.learningObjective: evaluate the shared pattern of Atlantic revolutions

questions.stem: Step back from Boston harbor, Paris streets, Haitian cane fields, and Andean passes: constitutions differ and slavery's fate differs, yet each rising denounced tyranny in liberty's name. Which shared pattern best describes all four?

stimulus.body: From Boston harbor to Paris streets, from Haitian cane fields to Andean passes, crowds and armies rose within a single lifetime. Each denounced tyranny in the language of liberty, each faced a bankrupt crown or a rigid order of ranks, and each claimed that a people might remake its government.
